citation: Kim S, Casement MD. The sweet spot of weekend catch-up sleep: U-shaped associations with internalizing symptoms in adolescents from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. Sleep. 2026;49(7):zsag113.
your_quote: Adolescents with moderate WCS (≤2 h) had lower odds of clinical level anxiety than those with consistent sleep (odds ratio = 0.49, confidence interval = 0.30 to 0.78, p = .003).
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (efetch, PMID 42023681); full text of Sleep 2026;49(7):zsag113 is paywalled and could not be retrieved, so extraction rests on the abstract's RESULTS sentence. Conversion: log_or = ln(0.49) = -0.713350. SE = (ln(0.78) - ln(0.30))/3.92 = (-0.248461 - (-1.203973))/3.92 = 0.955511/3.92 = 0.243753. Exposure match: the paper's 'moderate WCS' category is ≤2 h of weekend catch-up versus 'consistent sleep' (no catch-up), which is the closest available operationalisation of the target 1.0 h vs 0.0 h contrast; the paper does not report a per-hour or exactly-1-h estimate, so the category contrast is what I extracted. Sign: negative log OR because more (moderate) catch-up sleep was associated with LOWER odds of clinical-level anxiety. Note that the task's sign convention ('positive = elevated risk with short sleep') is defined for short-sleep exposures; here the exposure is weekend catch-up sleep, so I report the estimate exactly as published without flipping. n = 1867 adolescents in the ABCD analytic sample; the abstract does not report the number in each WCS category. Design: Fitbit-derived sleep and concurrent CBCL symptoms analysed with logistic/quadratic regression, i.e. cross-sectional association within a longitudinal cohort, hence cross_sectional / TX rather than a prospective tier.

citation: Fadnes LT, Celis-Morales C, Okland JM, Parra-Soto S, Livingstone KM, Ho FK, Pell JP, Balakrishna R, Sulo G, Vollset SE, Johansson KA. Life expectancy gains from dietary modifications: a comparative modeling study in 7 countries. Am J Clin Nutr. 2024;120(1):170-177.
your_note: Source: publisher PDF of Am J Clin Nutr 2024;120(1):170-177, Table 2 (row 'United States males (1.75 m, 70 kg)', age 40, column TD->OD = typical diet to longevity-optimized diet). Value 9.7 y with uncertainty interval 8.1-11.3 y. The same figure appears in the abstract: 'For 40-y-olds, estimated life expectancy gains ranged from 6.2 y (with uncertainty interval [UI]: 5.7, 7.5 y) for Chinese females to 9.7 y (UI: 8.1, 11.3 y) for United States males following sustained changes from typical country-specific dietary patterns to longevity-optimized dietary changes'. SE = (11.3 - 8.1)/3.92 = 3.2/3.92 = 0.816327, treating the modelled uncertainty interval as a 95% interval (it is a simulation UI, not a sampling CI, so this SE is only an approximation). your_n = null: this is a comparative modelling study (Food4HealthyLife) built on published dose-response meta-analyses and GBD background mortality, so there is no analytic sample for this estimate. Possible source of disagreement: the Discussion says 'for 40-y-old adults, changing to a longevity-optimized diet is projected to result in LE gains in the range of 6-8 y', which understates the US male value of 9.7 y given in both the abstract and Table 2; an extractor reading the Discussion could record 6-8 y instead.

citation: Dinges DF, Pack F, Williams K, Gillen KA, Powell JW, Ott GE, Aptowicz C, Pack AI. Cumulative sleepiness, mood disturbance, and psychomotor vigilance performance decrements during a week of sleep restricted to 4-5 hours per night. Sleep. 1997;20(4):267-277.
target_unit: hours of achieved nightly sleep, mean (SD 0.57)
your_quote: 16 healthy young adults had their sleep restricted 33% below habitual sleep duration, to an average 4.98 hours per night [standard deviation (SD) = 0.57] for seven consecutive nights.
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (efetch, PMID 9231952); Sleep 1997;20(4):267-277 full text is not open access, but the achieved-TST value and its SD are stated verbatim in the abstract. Value = 4.98 h achieved nightly sleep under the nominal 5-h dose, matching target_exposure_dose_h = 4.98. SE = SD/sqrt(n) = 0.57/sqrt(16) = 0.57/4 = 0.1425. The target referent of 7.43 h is consistent with the reported '33% below habitual sleep duration' (4.98/0.67 = 7.43 h habitual). Design: single-arm within-subject laboratory restriction with staff monitoring and actigraphy (no randomised comparison arm), which is why I judged RoB as some_concerns rather than low for this descriptive exposure-measurement quantity.

citation: Wild CJ, Nichols ES, Battista ME, Stojanoski B, Owen AM. Dissociable effects of self-reported daily sleep duration on high-level cognitive abilities. Sleep. 2018;41(12):zsy182.
your_quote: This figure shows, for example, that reasoning, verbal, and overall performance scores for participants who reportedly slept only 4 hours per night were on average 0.20, 0.20, and 0.26 SDs lower, respectively, than participants who slept the optimal amount (reasoning: t(10865) = 7.94, p < 0.001; verbal t(10865) = 7.19, p < 0.001, overall t(10865) = 10.55, p < 0.001).
your_note: Source: PMC6289236 full text (Sleep 2018;41(12):zsy182), Results. The verbal composite at a self-reported 4 h/night was 0.20 SD BELOW performance at the optimum, and the paper's estimated verbal optimum is 7.44 h ('The optimal amount of sleep was found to be 7.16 ... 7.44 ... and 7.38 ... hours for reasoning, verbal, and overall abilities, respectively'), which is exactly the target referent of 7.44 h. Sign: negative because performance is worse at the shorter sleep duration. SE = |g|/t = 0.20/7.19 = 0.027816 (the paper reports the t statistic for this contrast, not a CI). The estimate is a standardised difference from a fitted quadratic curve, i.e. a model-predicted difference in SD units rather than a two-group Hedges' g, so a small-sample bias correction (J) is not applicable. n = 10886 (final analytic sample: 'This resulted in final sample of 10886 participants'); the df of 10865 reflects the 20-column design matrix. Design: single-session online battery with self-reported habitual sleep over the past month, i.e. cross-sectional.

citation: Fondell E, Axelsson J, Franck K, Ploner A, Lekander M, Balter K, Gaines H. Short natural sleep is associated with higher T cell and lower NK cell activities. Brain, Behavior, and Immunity. 2011;25(7):1367-1375.
your_quote: Short sleep duration prior to blood draw (<7 h) was associated with 49% higher PHA-induced T cell function (95% CI 7/109%) and 30% lower NKCA compared with normal prior sleep (7-9 h) (95% CI -46/-8%).
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (efetch, PMID 21496482); Brain Behav Immun 2011;25(7):1367-1375 is paywalled (Elsevier) and could not be retrieved, so the percentage change and its CI come from the abstract. Conversion to the target log-ratio scale: +49% => ratio 1.49, ln(1.49) = 0.398776. CI 7% to 109% => ratios 1.07 and 2.09; SE = (ln(2.09) - ln(1.07))/3.92 = (0.737164 - 0.067659)/3.92 = 0.669505/3.92 = 0.170792. TARGET-SPEC CONCERN: target_scale is log_rr, but this quantity is a ratio of a continuous immune-function measure (PHA-induced T cell function per volume of whole blood), not a risk ratio, and a HIGHER value is not a 'risk'. I have kept the sign as published (positive = higher T cell function with short sleep); if the convention 'positive = elevated risk' is applied to an immune-activation outcome the sign is not interpretable. Exposure match: the paper's contrast is <7 h versus 7-9 h prior-night self-reported sleep, which is the categorical analogue of the target 6 h vs 8 h contrast. n = 36 participants (29 sampled on three consecutive mornings, 7 on one morning, i.e. 94 blood draws); the abstract does not state how many observations entered this particular model.

citation: Yoshiike T, Kawamura A, Utsumi T, Matsui K, Kuriyama K. A prospective study of the association of weekend catch-up sleep and sleep duration with mortality in middle-aged adults. Sleep Biol Rhythms. 2023 May 5;21(4):409-418.
your_quote: The regression analysis of TST-CUS classifications showed that compared to no CUS with normal sleep duration (≥ 390 min), 1-h CUS with normal sleep duration (≥ 390 min) was consistently associated with lower mortality (fully adjusted HR, 0.36; 95% CI 0.17–0.78), whereas 1-h CUS with short sleep duration (< 330 min) was consistently associated with higher mortality (fully adjusted HR, 1.84; 95% CI 1.08–3.14; Table 2)
your_note: Source: PMC10900010 full text (Sleep Biol Rhythms 2023;21(4):409-418), Results and Table 2. I extracted the joint catch-up-sleep x objective-sleep-duration cell that carries elevated risk with SHORT objective sleep: short weekend CUS (1 h) with PSG-measured TST < 330 min versus no CUS with TST >= 390 min, fully adjusted Model 2 HR = 1.84 (1.08-3.14). log_hr = ln(1.84) = 0.609766; SE = (ln(3.14) - ln(1.08))/3.92 = (1.144223 - 0.076961)/3.92 = 1.067262/3.92 = 0.272261. AMBIGUITY: the study reports three headline HRs for the catch-up x objective-sleep classification (0.48 [0.27-0.83] for 1-h CUS with normal TST >= 360 min under the primary cutoffs; 0.36 [0.17-0.78] for 1-h CUS with normal TST >= 390 min; 1.84 [1.08-3.14] for 1-h CUS with short TST < 330 min). Because target_exposure_type is habitual_short_sleep and the sign convention asks for elevated risk with short sleep, I selected the 1.84 estimate; an extractor selecting the protective cell would report -0.734 (0.48) or -1.022 (0.36) instead. n = 2028, the sample for the secondary-cutoff analysis (1100 participants with TST 330-390 min excluded); the specific contrast uses 211 exposed and 683 reference participants out of that 2028. Exposure is PSG-measured TST (objective) crossed with self-reported weekend catch-up sleep, so design/tier reflect the objective component.

citation: Zhang R, Luo L, Zhang L, Lin X, Wu C, Jiang F, Wang J. Genetically Supported Causality between Brain Structural Connectome and Sleep Duration in Children: A Two-Sample Mendelian Randomization Study. eNeuro. 2024;11(12):ENEURO.0267-24.2024.
target_unit: beta, sleep duration per SD of genetically instrumented structural connectivity
your_quote: Conversely, increased densities in the white-matter SC from the LH dorsal attention network to the thalamus (IVW: β = 0.14; 95% CI = [8.45 × 10−4, 0.27]; p = 0.05), the RH control network to the thalamus (IVW: β = 0.10; 95% CI = [0.01, 0.19]; p = 0.03), the RH default network to the thalamus (IVW: β = 0.08; 95% CI = [4.53 × 10−3, 0.16]; p = 0.04), the RH limbic network to the thalamus (IVW: β = 0.15; 95% CI = [0.05, 0.26]; p = 3.77 × 10−3), and the RH somatomotor network to the thalamus (IVW: β = 0.20; 95% CI = [0.07, 0.32]; p = 1.63 × 10−3) correlate with longer sleep durations in children.
your_note: Source: PMC11654012 full text (eNeuro 2024;11(12):ENEURO.0267-24.2024), Results and Table 2 (row 'RH SomMot network to thalamus white-matter SC', nsnp = 14, IVW 0.20 (0.07, 0.32), SE 0.06, p = 1.63e-3). Value = +0.20; the paper interprets it as hours: 'each standard deviation increase in the white-matter SC from the RH somatomotor network to the thalamus is associated with an increase in sleep duration by 0.20 h in children'. Positive sign = longer sleep, matching the target construct '...causes_longer_sleep'. SE = (0.32 - 0.07)/3.92 = 0.25/3.92 = 0.063776 per the CI rule; Table 2 reports SE = 0.06 (rounded), which is consistent. n = 10554: the outcome GWAS (sleep duration in children, Marinelli et al., PMID 27568811) sample; the exposure structural-connectome GWAS had 26,333 individuals and this instrument used 14 SNPs. An extractor could instead record 14 (SNPs) or 26333 (exposure GWAS) for n. Target_scale is 'smd' but the estimate is a beta in hours of sleep per SD of connectivity (i.e. only the exposure is standardised), as the target_unit itself states.

citation: Banks S, Van Dongen HPA, Maislin G, Dinges DF. Neurobehavioral dynamics following chronic sleep restriction: dose-response effects of one night for recovery. Sleep. 2010;33(8):1013-1026.
your_quote: Total sleep time was 1.88 h (0.04 h) in the 2-h TIB group, 3.84 h (0.03 h) in the 4-h TIB group, 5.74 h (0.04 h) in the 6-h TIB group, 7.51 h (0.10 h) in the 8-h TIB group, and 8.96 h (0.18 h) in 10-h TIB group.
your_note: Source: PMC2910531 full text (Sleep 2010;33(8):1013-1026), Results (recovery-night sleep). The maximum single-night recovery TST was 8.96 h at the largest recovery dose of 10 h TIB; the abstract states the same value ('recovery was incomplete at the 10 h TIB (8.96 h TST)'). SE = 0.18 h, the reported SEM for that group. n: I recorded 26, the number of participants contributing the paired 10-h REC vs B2 comparison ('Sleep-restricted subjects randomized to 10 h TIB on REC had a mean (+/- SEM) of 51.5 min (12.3 min) more TST than on their 10 h baseline night B2 (t25 = 4.17, P < 0.001)', df 25 => n 26). Other defensible values are 27 (the 10-h recovery subgroup size given in the Table 2 footnote) and 23 (subjects with complete PSG on all of B2/SR1/SR5/REC per the Figure 4 / correlation footnote); this is a likely source of disagreement. Design: the parent study randomised participants to one of six recovery doses, but the extracted quantity is a within-subject PSG-measured recovery sleep duration in the 10-h arm (target dose 10 h = referent 10 h), so I classified it as within-subject lab restriction/recovery.

citation: Lowe CJ, Safati A, Hall PA. The neurocognitive consequences of sleep restriction: A meta-analytic review. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews. 2017;80:586-604.
your_quote: Based on a sample of 61 studies, from 71 different populations, findings revealed a significant negative effect of sleep restriction on cognitive processing across cognitive domains (g=-0.383, p<0.001).
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (efetch, PMID 28757454). Neurosci Biobehav Rev 2017;80:586-604 is closed access (verified via Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar: no OA copy), so I could not read the full text or its confidence interval. Value = -0.383, the overall random-effects Hedges' g pooled across cognitive domains; the sign is already in the required direction (negative = worse performance under restriction). SE is NOT reported: I derived an UPPER BOUND from the reported p<0.001, SE <= |g|/z(0.001, two-sided) = 0.383/3.2905 = 0.1164. The true SE is almost certainly smaller (the domain-specific estimates were significant at p<0.001 with 61 studies), so treat 0.116 as a conservative bound rather than the published precision. your_n = null: the abstract reports 61 studies from 71 populations but no pooled participant count. RoB moderate: pooled across heterogeneous experimental protocols, domains and restriction doses, with age, time of day, cumulative days, sleep latency, sleepiness and sex all acting as significant moderators.

citation: Spiegel K, Tasali E, Penev P, Van Cauter E. Brief communication: Sleep curtailment in healthy young men is associated with decreased leptin levels, elevated ghrelin levels, and increased hunger and appetite. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2004;141(11):846-850.
target_unit: percent change in subjective hunger rating
your_quote: Sleep restriction was associated with average reductions in the anorexigenic hormone leptin (decrease, 18%; P = 0.04), elevations in the orexigenic factor ghrelin (increase, 28%; P < 0.04), and increased hunger (increase, 24%; P < 0.01) and appetite (increase, 23%; P = 0.01), especially for calorie-dense foods with high carbohydrate content (increase, 33% to 45%; P = 0.02).
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (efetch, PMID 15583226); Ann Intern Med 2004;141(11):846-850 full text is paywalled, so the percentage and p value come from the structured abstract. Value = +24 (percent increase in subjective hunger under 2 days of 4-h bedtimes versus 2 days of 10-h bedtimes), matching target_unit 'percent change in subjective hunger rating'; hunger is a 'higher is worse' outcome, so the positive sign denotes a worse outcome under restriction. SE is not reported. Derived UPPER BOUND from p<0.01 with a paired t test on n=12 (df=11, t_crit = 3.1058): SE <= 24/3.1058 = 7.73 percentage points. This is a weak bound and could easily disagree with a null or with a directly reported SEM in the full text. n = 12 healthy men. Design: the abstract states 'Randomized, 2-period, 2-condition crossover clinical study'; RoB some_concerns because sleep condition cannot be blinded and the order effects of a 2-period crossover in 12 subjects are not fully reported in the abstract.

citation: Livingston G, Huntley J, Liu KY, Costafreda SG, Selbaek G, Alladi S, Ames D, Banerjee S, Burns A, Brayne C, Fox NC, Ferri CP, Gitlin LN, Howard R, Kales HC, Kivimaki M, Larson EB, Nakasujja N, Rockwood K, Samus Q, Shirai K, Singh-Manoux A, Schneider LS, Walsh S, Yao Y, Sommerlad A, Mukadam N. Dementia prevention, intervention, and care: 2024 report of the Lancet standing Commission. Lancet. 2024 Aug 10;404(10452):572-628.
your_quote: In the million-woman study of 830,716 women (mean age 60 years at baseline) with a 17-year follow-up, there was a slightly higher risk of dementia (RR 1.08, 1.04-1.12) among those who reported shorter but not very short sleep duration (<7 hours).
your_note: Source: full text PDF of the 2024 Lancet standing Commission report (Lancet 2024;404(10452):572-628), 'Short sleep duration' subsection. log_rr = ln(1.08) = 0.076961; SE = (ln(1.12) - ln(1.04))/3.92 = (0.113329 - 0.039221)/3.92 = 0.074108/3.92 = 0.018905. Positive = elevated dementia risk with short (<7 h) sleep, consistent with the required sign convention. n = 830716 women. Exposure match: the Commission's '<7 hours' versus the normal-sleep referent corresponds to the target 6.5 h vs 7.5 h contrast. TARGET-SPEC CONCERN: livingston2024 is itself a commissioned narrative review/consensus report, and this RR is secondary-cited from the Million Women Study (Wong et al., reference 306 of the Commission). I set design/tier to describe the underlying evidence (prospective cohort with self-reported sleep duration, T5); an extractor who classifies the container document instead would record guideline_consensus / TX. RoB moderate: self-reported sleep, and the Commission itself flags reverse causation ('current evidence appears to indicate that short sleep duration may be associated with a small, increased' risk).

citation: Ong JL, Lo JC, Gooley JJ, Chee MW. EEG Changes across Multiple Nights of Sleep Restriction and Recovery in Adolescents: The Need for Sleep Study. Sleep. 2016;39(6):1233-1240.
your_quote: Although SWS duration was slightly elevated on M7 in the SR group (SR: 109.26 ± 3.33 min vs. Control: 97.17 ± 5.31 min; P = 0.03), mean SWS across manipulation nights did not differ between groups (SR: 101.10 ± 3.36 min vs. Control: 99.13 ± 5.42 min; P = 0.75).
your_note: Source: PMC4863211 full text (Sleep 2016;39(6):1233-1240), Results. The paper reports SWS in minutes, not a standardised effect, so I computed Hedges' g myself for the 5-h TIB (SR, n=29) vs 9-h TIB (Control, n=26) contrast averaged over the 7 manipulation nights. Arithmetic: SD = SEM x sqrt(n), so SD_SR = 3.36 x sqrt(29) = 18.094 and SD_Control = 5.42 x sqrt(26) = 27.637; pooled SD = sqrt((28 x 18.094^2 + 25 x 27.637^2)/53) = 23.0920; d = (101.10 - 99.13)/23.0920 = 0.08531; J = 1 - 3/(4 x 53 - 1) = 0.98578; g = 0.0841; SE(g) = sqrt(1/29 + 1/26 + g^2/(2 x 53)) = 0.27021. The implied t of 0.32 reproduces the paper's P = 0.75, which supports the SD back-calculation. SIGN: positive here means MORE SWS under restriction (SWS was preserved/slightly elevated); for a homeostatic sleep-architecture variable, 'negative = worse' is not meaningful, so the sign denotes direction of change only. AMBIGUITY: two other numbers could match 'slow_wave_sleep_minutes_at_5h_tib' - the M7-only between-group contrast (109.26 vs 97.17, g = 0.52) and the within-SR comparison of manipulation nights against the 9-h baseline night B3 (P = 0.76). n = 55 (29 SR + 26 Control in the sleep-macrostructure analyses).

citation: Kitamura S, Katayose Y, Nakazaki K, Motomura Y, Oba K, Katsunuma R, Terasawa Y, Enomoto M, Moriguchi Y, Hida A, Mishima K. Estimating individual optimal sleep duration and potential sleep debt. Sci Rep. 2016;6:35812.
your_quote: Among all participants, the mean HSD at home was 7.37 ± 0.27 h (range, 5.82–8.89 h).
your_note: Source: PMC5075948 full text (Sci Rep 2016;6:35812), Results ('Habitual sleep duration'). Habitual sleep duration (HSD) was measured at home by wrist actigraphy plus sleep diary for approximately 2 weeks, matching target_exposure_duration_days = 14. Value = 7.37 h; the reported +/- 0.27 h is a standard error, not an SD (0.27 x sqrt(15) = 1.05 h, which is consistent with the observed range 5.82-8.89 h), so your_se = 0.27. n = 15 healthy young Japanese men. Possible disagreement: the Discussion rounds this to 'The mean at-home sleep time (i.e., HSD) was 7.3 h in the participants', so an extractor may record 7.3. This is a descriptive normative quantity, hence normative_descriptive / TX; RoB some_concerns given the small single-sex convenience sample despite objective measurement.

citation: Wang H, Sun J, Sun M, Liu N, Wang M. Relationship of sleep duration with the risk of stroke incidence and stroke mortality: an updated systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies. Sleep Med. 2022 Feb;90:267-278.
your_quote: Meta-analysis showed that short sleep was linked to an increased risk of stroke incidence and stroke mortality (RR: 1.33, 95% CI: 1.19-1.49 and RR: 1.37, 95% CI: 1.16-1.62 respectively).
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (efetch, PMID 35245890); Sleep Med 2022;90:267-278 is paywalled (Elsevier) and no OA copy was available, so the pooled RR comes from the abstract. Stroke-mortality estimate for short sleep: RR = 1.37 (1.16-1.62). log_rr = ln(1.37) = 0.314811; SE = (ln(1.62) - ln(1.16))/3.92 = (0.482426 - 0.148420)/3.92 = 0.334006/3.92 = 0.085206. Positive = elevated stroke mortality with short sleep, as required. your_n = null: the abstract reports 12 reports contributing to the stroke-mortality analysis (20 articles / 27 reports overall) but no pooled participant count. AMBIGUITY: the paper contains both a categorical (short vs normal) pairwise meta-analysis and a spline dose-response analysis. Because target_scale is a single log RR with no dose specified, I took the categorical short-sleep estimate; an extractor taking a per-hour dose-response estimate would report a very different number, and would arguably code the design as dose_response_meta_analysis. Tier T5 because the pooled evidence is prospective cohorts with self-reported sleep duration.

citation: Klingenberg L, Chaput JP, Holmback U, Visby T, Jennum P, Nikolic M, Astrup A, Sjodin A. Acute sleep restriction reduces insulin sensitivity in adolescent boys. Sleep. 2013 Jul 1;36(7):1085-1090.
target_unit: % lower Matsuda index in short-sleep vs long-sleep condition
your_quote: The homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) index was 65% higher (P = 0.002) and the Matsuda index was 28% lower (P = 0.007) in the SS condition compared to the LS condition.
your_note: Source: PMC3669075 full text (Sleep 2013;36(7):1085-1090), abstract Results. Value = 28, reported exactly in the units named by the target ('% lower Matsuda index in short-sleep vs long-sleep condition'); expressed as a signed percentage change it would be -28%, which is a plausible source of sign disagreement. SE is not reported. Derived from the exact p value: paired t test, n = 21, df = 20, p = 0.007 => t = 3.0298, so SE = 28/3.0298 = 9.24 percentage points. This assumes the p value came from a simple paired t test on the percentage difference, so treat it as approximate. n = 21 healthy normal-weight adolescent boys. Design: 'A randomized crossover design, with 2 experimental conditions: 3 consecutive nights of short sleep (SS, 4 h/night) and long sleep (LS, 9 h/night) duration', matching the target 4 h vs 9 h over 3 days. RoB some_concerns: no blinding, and mid-sleep time was not synchronised between conditions (03:00-07:00 vs 22:00-07:00), so circadian displacement is confounded with sleep duration - the authors acknowledge this.

citation: Lundahl A, Kidwell KM, Van Dyk TR, Nelson TD. A meta-analysis of the effect of experimental sleep restriction on youth's attention and hyperactivity. Developmental Neuropsychology. 2015;40(3):104-121.
your_quote: Six samples (N = 279) examined the difference in attention between extended sleep (sleep extension) and sleep restriction. The overall effect size of −0.37 was significant (95% CI: −0.55 to −0.19, p < .0001) and represents a small to medium effect size
your_note: Source: full article text of Dev Neuropsychol 2015;40(3):104-121. The Taylor & Francis version is paywalled and there is no PMC/OA copy, so I read a verbatim PDF-text reproduction of the published article (docksci mirror) after confirming the title, authors, journal, pagination, DOI and abstract match the PubMed record exactly. In that text the CI is split across a page break ('95% CI: −0.55 to' / '−0.19, p < .0001'), which I have joined in the quote. Value = -0.37, the random-effects pooled Hedges' g for attention, extended sleep versus restricted sleep - exactly the target contrast (target_exposure_type = sleep_extension). Sign is already negative (the paper states 'negative effect size represents poorer performance after experimental sleep restriction'). SE = (-0.19 - (-0.55))/3.92 = 0.36/3.92 = 0.091837. n = 279 across 6 independent samples. ALTERNATIVE CANDIDATE: trim-and-fill correction for funnel asymmetry gave an adjusted g of -0.26 (95% CI -0.46 to -0.05); an extractor preferring the bias-adjusted value would record -0.26 (SE 0.105). Also note the restriction-vs-normal-sleep attention estimate is a different number (-0.19, 95% CI -0.34 to -0.03). RoB moderate: publication bias detected, I^2 = 67.3%, and the authors used between-groups effect sizes for predominantly within-subject studies (conservative, biased toward zero).

citation: Bubu OM, Brannick M, Mortimer J, Umasabor-Bubu O, Sebastiao YV, Wen Y, Schwartz S, Borenstein AR, Wu Y, Morgan D, Anderson WM. Sleep, Cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sleep. 2017 Jan 1;40(1):zsw032.
your_quote: Individuals with sleep problems had a 1.55 (95% CI: 1.25-1.93), 1.65 (95% CI: 1.45-1.86), and 3.78 (95% CI: 2.27-6.30) times higher risk of AD, cognitive impairment, and preclinical AD than individuals without sleep problems, respectively.
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (efetch, PMID 28364458); Sleep 2017;40(1):zsw032 full text could not be retrieved (Unpaywall points to an academic.oup.com PDF that returns a bot-block page, and there is no PMC copy). Preclinical AD estimate: RR = 3.78 (2.27-6.30). log_rr = ln(3.78) = 1.329724; SE = (ln(6.30) - ln(2.27))/3.92 = (1.840550 - 0.819780)/3.92 = 1.020770/3.92 = 0.260400. Positive = elevated risk with sleep problems, consistent with the convention. your_n = null: the meta-analysis included 27 studies with 69,216 participants and 52 RR estimates in total, but the abstract does not report how many studies or participants contributed the preclinical-AD estimate specifically. Exposure is 'any sleep problem/disorder' (not specifically short sleep duration), which matches target_exposure_type = other; tier T5 because the pooled evidence is observational cohorts with largely self-reported sleep problems.

citation: Li Y, Pan A, Wang DD, Liu X, Dhana K, Franco OH, Kaptoge S, Di Angelantonio E, Stampfer M, Willett WC, Hu FB. Impact of healthy lifestyle factors on life expectancies in the US population. Circulation. 2018;138(4):345-355.
your_quote: The multivariable-adjusted HRs for mortality in adults with five compared with zero low-risk factors were 0.26 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.22–0.31) for all-cause mortality, 0.35 (95% CI: 0.27–0.45) for cancer mortality and 0.18 (95% CI: 0.12–0.26) for CVD mortality.
your_note: Source: PMC6207481 full text (Circulation 2018;138(4):345-355), abstract Results; the same estimate appears in the Results text ('A combination of five low-risk lifestyle factors was associated with a HR (95% CI) of 0.26 (0.22-0.31) for all-cause mortality'). log_hr = ln(0.26) = -1.347074; SE = (ln(0.31) - ln(0.22))/3.92 = (-1.171183 - (-1.514128))/3.92 = 0.342945/3.92 = 0.087486. The negative sign means lower mortality with five versus zero low-risk lifestyle factors; the task's 'positive = elevated risk with short sleep' convention does not apply because target_exposure_type is 'other' (a lifestyle comparator), so I report the published direction. n = 123219 = 78,865 (Nurses' Health Study) + 44,354 (Health Professionals Follow-up Study), with 42,167 deaths over up to 34 years. Design: prospective cohorts with self-reported diet, smoking, activity, alcohol and BMI.

citation: Bouman EJ, Beulens JWJ, Groeneveld L, de Kruijk RS, Schoonmade LJ, Remmelzwaal S, Elders PJM, Rutters F. The association between social jetlag and parameters of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Sleep Research. 2023;32(3):e13770.
your_quote: High quality studies showed that having social jetlag compared to no social jetlag was significantly associated with higher body mass index in 20 studies (0.49 kg/m2 , 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.21-0.77; I2 = 100%), higher waist circumference in seven studies (1.11 cm, 95% CI 0.42-1.80; I2 = 25%), higher systolic blood pressure in 10 studies (0.37 mmHg, 95% CI 0.00-0.74; I2 = 94%) and higher glycated haemoglobin in 12 studies (0.42%, 95% CI 0.12- 0.72; I2 = 100%).
your_note: Source: PubMed abstract (efetch, PMID 36351658); J Sleep Res 2023;32(3):e13770 full text was not retrievable (Wiley returned a bot-challenge page for both the article and PDF URLs). Value = 0.37 mmHg higher systolic blood pressure with social jetlag versus none, pooled across 10 high-quality studies. SE = (0.74 - 0.00)/3.92 = 0.74/3.92 = 0.188776; note the reported lower bound is 0.00 (rounded to 2 dp), so this SE is slightly imprecise. your_n = null: the abstract gives the number of studies (10) but not the pooled participant count. AMBIGUITY: the abstract reports the estimate restricted to high-quality studies; the full text may also report an all-studies pooled SBP estimate, which would be a different number. Tier TX and RoB high because the authors state the evidence is 'low' level and 'mostly based on cross-sectional data', with I^2 = 94% for this outcome and no reduction in heterogeneity on sensitivity analysis.

citation: Klerman EB, Dijk DJ. Age-related reduction in the maximal capacity for sleep - implications for insomnia. Current Biology. 2008;18(15):1118-1123.
target_unit: hours of total daily sleep time (maximal capacity / satiated sleep)
your_quote: The asymptotic value for TST for younger subjects was 8.9 hours (C.I. 8.1-9.7 hours) (p=0.009 vs. older) and was not achieved until approximately the fifth 24-hour of extended sleep opportunity.
your_note: Source: PMC2582347 full text (Curr Biol 2008;18(15):1118-1123), Results ('Asymptotic duration of sleep, NREM sleep and REM sleep') and Table 1. Value = 8.9 h total daily sleep (maximal capacity / satiated sleep) in the 35 younger subjects, estimated by mixed-model exponential regression across extended sleep opportunities. your_se = 0.4, the standard error reported in the abstract and Table 1 ('asymptotic values that were 1.5 hour shorter in older (7.4 +/- 0.4 s.e.m., hour) than younger subjects (8.9 +/- 0.4)'); the CI-based rule gives the same answer, (9.7 - 8.1)/3.92 = 0.408. The target dose of 16 h corresponds to the protocol's daily sleep opportunity of 12 h at night plus 4 h in the afternoon, and 7 days is within the protocol's 3-7 day range. n = 35 younger subjects (18 older subjects excluded from this estimate). ALTERNATIVE CANDIDATE: for younger subjects restricted to the same habitual-sleep-duration range as the older subjects the asymptote was 9.2 h (CI 8.3-10.1).

citation: Blattner MS, Panigrahi SK, Toedebusch CD, Hicks TJ, McLeland JS, Banks IR, Schaibley C, Ovod V, Mawuenyega KG, Bateman RJ, Holtzman DM, Landsness EC, Lucey BP. Increased cerebrospinal fluid amyloid-beta during sleep deprivation in healthy middle-aged adults is not due to stress or circadian disruption. Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. 2020;75(2):471-482.
target_unit: % difference in overnight CSF Abeta42 concentration, sleep-deprived minus control
your_quote: For Aβ42, the overnight estimated difference over the same period was +8.6% (SE 3.1, 95% CI 2.4 – 14.9, p=0.007).
your_note: Source: PMC7246155 full text (J Alzheimers Dis 2020;75(2):471-482), Results. Value = +8.6% overnight difference in CSF Abeta42 between the sleep-deprived and control conditions, exactly the quantity named by the target. your_se = 3.1 as reported directly by the paper; the CI rule would give (14.9 - 2.4)/3.92 = 3.19, essentially the same. n = 11 participants ('Five of the 11 participants completed both the control and sleep-deprived conditions ... Six additional participants completed only one group (3 control, 3 sleep-deprived)'), i.e. 8 control and 8 sleep-deprived condition-visits; the cosinor models report F tests with (1,7) df, so an extractor might instead record 8 or 16. Design: participants were randomised to sleep deprivation or normal-sleep control with partial repetition after a 4-6 month washout, so it is a randomised parallel-group study with a partial crossover element rather than a true crossover (the authors themselves suggest future 'randomized crossover designs'). Possible disagreement: the paper's abstract rounds this to 'approximately 10%'. RoB some_concerns: n = 11, light exposure uncontrolled, no adjustment for multiple comparisons.

citation: James SA, Erickson DJ, Lammert S, Widome R. School start time delays and high school educational outcomes: Evidence from the START/LEARN study. Journal of Adolescence. 2023;95(4):751-763.
your_quote: | GPA, Wayzata weighted | 0.02 (−0.03, 0.07) | 0.01 (−0.03, 0.06) | −0.0005 (−0.05, 0.05) | 0.17*** (0.11, 0.23) | 0.14*** (0.07, 0.21) | [columns: Pre-baseline to baseline | Baseline to follow-up 1a | Baseline to follow-up 1b | Baseline to follow-up 2a | Baseline to follow-up 2b]
your_note: Source: PMC10257742 full text (J Adolesc 2023;95(4):751-763), Table 3, difference-in-differences panel. The target 'gpa_did_year2_fall_weighted' corresponds to the 'Baseline to follow-up 2a' column (Fall 2017, i.e. the second year of follow-up) in the weighted-GPA row: DiD = 0.17 (95% CI 0.11, 0.23), p < 0.001. SE = (0.23 - 0.11)/3.92 = 0.12/3.92 = 0.030612. SIGN: +0.17 GPA points is the effect of the LATER start time (which increased objectively measured sleep by about 40 min/night); if the convention is to express the estimate per shorter sleep the sign flips to -0.17. This is the most likely source of disagreement on this row, since target_exposure_type is 'chronic_restriction' while the published contrast is delayed-start (more sleep) versus early-start. The matching unweighted-GPA DiD is 0.08 (0.02, 0.13). n = 2153 adolescents in the START/LEARN cohort. Design: difference-in-differences natural experiment (schools not randomised), hence quasi_experiment / T2; RoB moderate because only one pre-treatment period is available for the parallel-trends assumption and follow-up time is confounded with grade progression.

citation: Rabat A, Gomez-Merino D, Roca-Paixao L, Bougard C, Van Beers P, Dispersyn G, Guillard M, Bourrilhon C, Drogou C, Arnal PJ, Sauvet F, Leger D, Chennaoui M. Differential Kinetics in Alteration and Recovery of Cognitive Processes from a Chronic Sleep Restriction in Young Healthy Men. Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience. 2016;10:95.
your_quote: | Daily score | 3.22 ± 0.31 | 3.82 ± 0.32 | 4.66 ± 0.31### | 4.73 ± 0.43### | 2.85 ± 0.42 | 2.92 ± 0.40 | [columns: Baseline: B2 | Restriction: SR1 | Restriction: SR4 | Restriction: SR7 | Recovery: R3 | Recovery: R13; ###p < 0.001 vs B2]
your_note: Source: PMC4876616 full text (Front Behav Neurosci 2016;10:95), Table 1 and Results. TARGET-SPEC CONCERN: the construct as named ('subjective_sleepiness_kss_plateaus_between_day_4_and_day_7') describes the SHAPE of the KSS time course, not a single effect size - the paper's point is that daily KSS was 4.66 at SR4 and 4.73 at SR7, i.e. essentially unchanged (that between-day difference is g = 0.05). Since target_exposure_dose_h/referent_h/duration_days specify 4 h vs 8 h over 7 days, I extracted the day-7 restriction versus baseline contrast for daily KSS instead. Arithmetic: SDs from SEM x sqrt(12): B2 = 0.31 x 3.4641 = 1.0739, SR7 = 0.43 x 3.4641 = 1.4896; pooled SD = sqrt((1.0739^2 + 1.4896^2)/2) = 1.2985; d = (4.73 - 3.22)/1.2985 = 1.16292; J = 1 - 3/(4 x 11 - 1) = 0.93023; g = 1.0818. SIGN: reported as NEGATIVE (-1.08) because a higher KSS score is greater sleepiness, i.e. a worse outcome under restriction, per the stated convention; the raw arithmetic gives +1.08 on the KSS scale. SE = 0.44 is an independent-groups approximation, sqrt(1/12 + 1/12 + g^2/(2 x 22)) = 0.43962; the design is within-subject and the paper reports no pre-post correlation, so the true paired SE is smaller and 0.44 is conservative. The corresponding SR4 vs B2 value is g = 1.25. n = 12; RoB some_concerns (single-arm within-subject laboratory protocol without a parallel control, non-parametric tests, subjective outcome).

citation: Creswell JD, Tumminia MJ, Price S, Sefidgar Y, Cohen S, Ren Y, Brown J, Dey AK, Dutcher JM, Villalba D, Mankoff J, Xu X, Creswell K, Doryab A, Mattingly S, Striegel A, Hachen D, Martinez G, Lovett MC. Nightly sleep duration predicts grade point average in the first year of college. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2023;120(8):e2209123120.
target_unit: GPA points (4.0 scale) per hour LESS nightly sleep
your_quote: A subsequent pooled analysis aggregating all four confirmatory studies showed that greater early-term total sleep time (TST) was significantly associated with higher GPA when controlling for previous-term GPA (N = 557, β = 0.001, p < .01) which corresponds to a 0.07 improvement in GPA for every additional hour of nightly sleep
your_note: Source: PMC9974458 full text (PNAS 2023;120(8):e2209123120), Results; the significance statement puts it in the target's direction: 'Every hour of lost total average nightly sleep was associated with a 0.07 reduction in end-of-term GPA.' Value = -0.07 GPA points per hour LESS nightly sleep (target_unit), i.e. -0.07 = -(+0.07 per extra hour); negative denotes the worse outcome with shorter sleep. Note the published per-minute coefficient is beta = 0.001 (rounded to 3 dp), which would imply 0.06 per hour; the authors' own conversion is 0.07 per hour, so the underlying beta must be about 0.00117 - a rounding-driven source of disagreement (0.06 vs 0.07). SE is not reported (Table 2 gives beta, R^2 and p only). Derived UPPER BOUND from p<.01: SE <= 0.07/z(0.01) = 0.07/2.5758 = 0.027176. n = 557 (pooled confirmatory Studies 2-5); the discovery study (Study 1) had N = 77 with beta = 0.002, and the fully covariate-adjusted pooled model also had N = 557. Design: month-long wrist actigraphy/Fitbit sleep early in term prospectively predicting end-of-term GPA with previous-term GPA controlled - observational but with objective exposure measurement, hence prospective_cohort_objective / T4. RoB moderate: non-randomised, residual confounding (e.g. depression, substance use) acknowledged by the authors.
